reconcile.connective: Commentators harmonize by distinguishing senses of "judge": the prohibition targets censorious, hypocritical, private condemnation, while civil and corrective righteous judgment remains commanded.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, who catalogs this in the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, presses that the texts issue flatly opposing commandments on whether believers should judge others at all.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013; "Should we judge others?" contradiction list)

excerpts.excerpt_text: He speaketh not here of civil judgments, and therefore by the word, forgive, is meant that good nature, which the Christians use in suffering and pardoning wrongs.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the tension by restricting Christ's "judge not" to a sense other than civil/legal judging, which Lev 19:15 and 1 Cor command.

excerpts.excerpt_text: There are those whose office it is to judge - magistrates and ministers. Christ, though he made not himself a Judge, yet came not to unmake them, for by him princes decree justice; but this is directed to private persons, to his disciples, who shall hereafter sit on thrones judging, but not now.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Distinguishes the office of judging (left intact, covering 1 Cor 5-6) from the private censoriousness Jesus forbids, dissolving the apparent conflict.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Judge not, &c.—that is, Rise above the letter into the spirit of the law.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Reads John 7:24's "judge righteous judgment" as the corrective complement to "judge not" - both aim at the law's spirit, not opposite rules.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Matthew 7:1
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this passage directly, harmonizing it by distinguishing the magistrate's/minister's office of judging from the private, censorious judging Christ prohibits.
